body.text: Since the February 2021 military coup, Myanmar has found itself increasingly isolated and forgotten on the global stage. For the people of Myanmar, who have endured years of brutal military suppression, Beijing’s continued engagement with the junta has fueled deep-seated resentment. Public sentiment has understandably skewed toward a skeptic and often hostile posture, driven by boycotts, protests, and widespread hostility.

While this moral outrage is justified on the streets, allowing it to dictate the country’s foreign policy would be a strategic trap for Myanmar’s political leadership. If the democratic resistance hopes to outmaneuver the military regime and secure a sovereign, federal democratic future, it must replace emotional anti-Chinese sentiment with a mature, calculated approach toward its powerful northern neighbor. Myanmar does not need an anti-China position; it desperately needs a China-critical policy.

However, suggesting that Myanmar needs a sensible China policy presents a problem in itself. The country is deeply entrenched in a civil war that is consuming it from the inside out. Each year, the United Nations faces a dilemma in determining who legitimately represents Myanmar. Whenever the Credentials Committee meets in New York, the U.N. is torn between two competing entities: Kyaw Moe Tun, the defiant diplomat for the National Unity Government (NUG), and whoever Naypyidaw and Min Aung Hlaing have lobbied for. Therefore, the question remains: whose “Myanmar” are we talking about when we discuss its foreign policy? This article will discuss the nature of both.

The international response has been equally fractured in dealing with Myanmar. The United States maintains a facade of condemnation of the Naypyidaw regime and pays lip service to the democratic resistance, yet has begun to engage the military-backed government via backroom deals and quiet engagements. More alarmingly, Washington’s Integrated Country Strategy on Myanmar explicitly outlines the Trump administration’s intention to expand its working relationship with Min Aung Hlaing’s regime. This signals a more consequential shift in Washington’s approach than its public rhetoric might suggest. ASEAN remains in a state of paralysis, playing an inconsistent game of carrots and sticks with the military while largely ignoring the resistance forces that now control sizable chunks of the country.

Meanwhile, China acting strictly on its own strategic logic maintains a layered and relatively coherent approach. Beijing continues to engage with all levels of Myanmar’s political landscape, including the military, ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) and the National League for Democracy (NLD).

China’s hand was highly visible during the Operation 1027 offensive in late 2023 and early 2024, when it worked with the EAOs in the Three Brotherhood Alliance to eradicate scam centers and rein in renegade warlords in northern and northeastern Myanmar. At the same time, Beijing has endorsed Min Aung Hlaing’s bid for the presidency and recognized his planned elections, all while continuing to acknowledge the imprisoned Aung San Suu Kyi as a long-standing friend of China. The NLD and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) maintained party-to-party contact after the coup and even after the military forcibly dissolved the NLD, the CCP kept its channels open, according to party insiders.

Aung San Suu Kyi herself has allegedly instructed the remnant and scattered NLD senior personnel on continuing their engagement with CCP, according to my personal communication with a party insider. Her alleged exact words, the insider said, were to contact the CCP and maintain good faith engagement whenever the two sides met.

Because China is engaging across the board, whoever claims the mantle of Myanmar’s legitimate government, whether the NUG or the new Steering Committee for Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), must match Beijing’s pragmatism. Reacting to China’s engagement with the junta with purely emotional, blanket “anti-China” sentiment is a strategic dead end.

Yet, the democratic resistance’s own China policy has been highly inconsistent. At times, its rhetoric has been unnecessarily hostile; at other times, attempts to court Beijing come across as insincere, leading China to largely dismiss these efforts.

Take, for example, the NUG’s Foreign Minister Zin Mar Aung. Her messaging has swung back and forth between sharply criticizing Beijing for its support of Naypyidaw and making awkward appeals to the CCP’s own revolutionary origins. This inconsistency is especially glaring given that the NUG actually published a relatively measured policy document regarding its position on China in January 2024. However, in practice, this paper has been largely ignored by both Zin Mar Aung and NUG cadres. It was never consistently communicated in the public sphere, nor was it ever effectively instrumentalized in diplomatic engagements with Beijing. Instead of serving as a guiding strategic doctrine, it quickly faded into digital obscurity, leaving the NUG under-engaged and largely sidelined in Beijing’s strategic calculus.

Other NUG ministers fare no better when asked about their stance on Beijing. This damning lack of a coherent policy is glaringly obvious when self-identified NUG-supporting diaspora groups organize and join broader anti-China rallies. Such moves are careless and strategically counterproductive. The most striking example occurred during President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States last September, where Myanmar diaspora groups joined forces with Tibetan and Uyghur interest groups to protest against China.

According to an anonymous former NUG staffer, the crowds even included family members of serving NUG officials and anti-China rallies of Myanmar diaspora abroad are often coordinated by close NUG associates. One cannot underestimate the reach of Chinese intelligence at these events, and Beijing is undoubtedly taking notes.

This is not to mention the Chiang Mai-based NGO-industrial complex fanning anti-Chinese rhetoric, and its failed attempt to court the Milk Tea Alliance, an anti-PRC activist coalition consisting mainly of exiled Hong Kong activists and Taiwanese pro-democracy activists. These actions represent just a few of the self-sabotaging moves the NUG and democratic resistance has made by letting emotional activism dictate its relationship with China.

Things are not so much different in Naypyidaw camp as well, with Min Aung Hlaing’s wild swings in search for strategic partnerships. Since the 2021 coup, Min Aung Hlaing has enthusiastically courted Moscow, albeit after a series of indifferent engagements and cold shoulders from Beijing. Then came Operation 1027, which greatly damaged his regime and compromised the military’s air of invincibility in Myanmar.

The rapprochement with China was solidified during and in the aftermath of Operation 1027. Beijing reportedly blessed him with the go-ahead for his planned 2025-2026 elections, hoping that a facade of political transition would bring some predictability and stabilize his government. Beijing did favor Min Aung Hlaing for a brief period earlier this year, reining in the Three Brotherhood Alliance, providing diplomatic backing for the transition, and finally granting Min Aung Hlaing an audience with President Xi in June 2026.

However, the latest turn of events between Beijing and Naypyidaw highlights the fragility of their relationship. Following a series of low-intensity engagements between the United States and regime officials, Min Aung Hlaing has begun to advocate reengagement with the West. “It would be ideal if the U.S. could cooperate with us in fostering the peace, stability, and development essential for our people to successfully realize a fully democratic state”, he told TIME in an otherwise highly damaging interview in September.

This apparent pivot clearly struck a nerve in Beijing. In response, Special Envoy Deng Xijun, who is highly influential and instrumental in brokering ceasefire deals between the Myanmar military and ethnic armed groups, publicly raised the need for high-level autonomy in Myanmar.

In retaliation, the regime quickly responded by activating anti-Chinese sentiment through its pro-military rally groups and propaganda outlets. It was not for the first time. At the height of Operation 1027, these exact groups had organized anti-Chinese protests across the country, events that could never have taken place without explicit military approval and coordination.

This state-sponsored hostility has increasingly spilled into the open. Prominent figures within the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), such as Hla Swe, recently entered into a feud with the pro-Beijing Chinese academic Zhao Jin. This came after Zhao criticized regime-adjacent and nominally independent Eleven Media outlet for an article attacking Deng Xijun’s remarks. Eleven media and Zhao exchanged a brief public spat over the Chinese position regarding Myanmar politics.

While Zhao’s remarks on Myanmar affairs left in poor taste in the mouths of the Myanmar audience on occasions in the past , Myanmar military propaganda outlets have largely ignored her remarks before.

Currently, Min Aung Hlaing is actively amplifying this anti-Chinese tone among pro-military extremist groups. The regime is opportunistically attacking the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army, a member of the Three Brotherhood Alliance, and its troubling Sinicization practices in the areas it controls in northern Shan State. State propaganda is now aggressively painting these resistance forces not as domestic revolutionaries, but as foreigners and Chinese renegades.

This author hopes that such political saber-rattling does not escalate into full-scale communal riots and unrest targeted at the ethnic Chinese community in Myanmar. Orchestrating this kind of covert, state-sponsored violence is a dark tactic the military has historically excelled at, as the world witnessed with their campaigns against the Rohingyas and the wider Muslim population. After all, Myanmar is not immune from anti-Chinese communal violence, as demonstrated by the 1967 anti-Chinese riots in Yangon.
These developments clearly show that the Myanmar military regime is an entirely unreliable partner for the kind of strategic stability China prefers to foster in the region.

Consequently, the two competing nodes of governance in Myanmar remain trapped in a state of cognitive dissonance when it comes to dealing with China. The junta swings between desperate submission and manufactured xenophobia, while the democratic resistance oscillates between moral outrage and awkward appeasement. If the resistance wants to gain a definitive strategic edge through its engagement with Beijing, it must abandon emotional activism and incoherent blunders in favor of a unified, China-critical policy.

Adopting a China-critical policy does not mean reducing Myanmar to a client state. Instead, the democratic resistance must anchor this policy in three pragmatic areas. First, on the economic front, the resistance must acknowledge the strategic reality of Beijing’s infrastructure projects and guarantee the safety of Chinese assets in the country. In exchange, they must demand an end to unregulated resource extraction and insist on good-faith negotiations aimed at purging bad actors.. Ironically, these are some of the points already tackled in the NUG’s own position paper, pointing to the need for following what it has already advocated.

Second, regarding border security, the resistance must directly challenge Beijing’s definition of stability and highlight Min Aung Hlaing as the main potential threat to it. The resistance must clearly argue that long-term stability is only possible under a popular federal democratic system, rather than a volatile and fractured landscape of junta-aligned warlords. Finally, the most crucial element is coherent messaging. Speaking to Beijing with a consistent, coordinated, coherent voice elevates the resistance from a collection of fragmented, emotional proxies to a legitimate, sovereign counterpart.

To conclude, it is vital to recognize that Min Aung Hlaing’s recent anti-Chinese saber-rattling does not constitute a China-critical policy. The two positions are not equally proportional. The junta’s rhetoric is a desperate, manufactured distraction, whereas a true China-critical stance is built on the establishment of firm strategic boundaries. Moving forward, the Myanmar resistance must clearly and sustainably communicate this distinction. The democratic forces must consistently demonstrate to Beijing that scrutinizing Chinese state policies and protecting national sovereignty does not equate to an anti-Chinese agenda.
